title: 1 Chronicles 12:23–40
context: The Chronicler lists the armed men who came to Hebron, tribe by tribe, to turn Saul’s kingdom over to David according to the LORD’s word. The numbers are given as the text states them; they are large, and interpreters read them in more than one way, including views that some terms rendered “thousand” may refer to military units rather than exact counts. Issachar’s men are said to understand the times, and Zebulun’s to be not of double heart. All come with a perfect heart to make David king over all Israel, and they feast for three days with provisions brought from as far as Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali, for there was joy in Israel.

verses.text: These are the numbers of the heads of those who were armed for war, who came to David to Hebron to turn the kingdom of Saul to him, according to the LORD’s word.
verses.arminianNotes: These are the numbers of those who came to David at Hebron to turn Saul’s kingdom to him, according to the LORD’s word. Arminian readers note the people’s active role in bringing about what God had promised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fulfillment of God’s word as the controlling idea of the Chronicler’s account. Both traditions read the verse as introducing a tribal list that shows all Israel coming together under David.

verses.text: The children of Judah who bore shield and spear were six thousand eight hundred, armed for war.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah sends six thousand eight hundred armed with shield and spear. Arminian readers note that David’s own tribe is listed first, though its number is smaller than some others in the list.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Judah’s place at the head of the list as fitting its role as the royal tribe. Shared ground: the numbers are given as the text states them, and both traditions note that interpreters read such figures in different ways.

verses.text: Of the children of Simeon, mighty men of valor for the war: seven thousand one hundred.
verses.arminianNotes: Simeon sends seven thousand one hundred mighty men of valor. Arminian readers note that Simeon, whose territory lay within Judah’s, is represented by a substantial force of its own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inclusion of every tribe as part of the Chronicler’s emphasis on all Israel. Both traditions read the number as given, without speculation about how it was counted or what units it represents.

verses.text: Of the children of Levi: four thousand six hundred.
verses.arminianNotes: Levi sends four thousand six hundred. Arminian readers note that the priestly tribe also takes part in making David king, showing support from those responsible for Israel’s worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Levites’ presence as fitting the Chronicler’s interest in worship and the temple. Shared ground: the number is given as the text states it, and both traditions read it as part of the larger tribal list.

verses.text: Jehoiada was the leader of the household of Aaron; and with him were three thousand seven hundred,
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoiada, leader of the household of Aaron, comes with three thousand seven hundred. Arminian readers note that the priestly family is named separately within Levi, honoring its distinct role.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that whether this Jehoiada is Benaiah’s father is uncertain. Both traditions read the verse as recording priestly support for David, without resolving questions of identity the text leaves open.

verses.text: and Zadok, a young man mighty of valor, and of his father’s house twenty-two captains.
verses.arminianNotes: Zadok, a young man mighty of valor, comes with twenty-two captains of his father’s house. Arminian readers note that many connect him with the later priest Zadok, though the verse does not say so.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in Zadok’s early support a hint of the role his line would have in Israel’s worship. Shared ground: both traditions hedge the identification, reading the verse as honoring a young leader.

verses.text: Of the children of Benjamin, Saul’s relatives: three thousand, for until then, the greatest part of them had kept their allegiance to Saul’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Benjamin sends three thousand, since most had remained loyal to Saul’s house until then. Arminian readers note the honesty of the account, which admits that Saul’s tribe was slow to support David.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the smaller number as reflecting the difficult transition from Saul’s house to David’s. Both traditions read the verse as a realistic note within a list that otherwise stresses unity.

verses.text: Of the children of Ephraim: twenty thousand eight hundred, mighty men of valor, famous men in their fathers’ houses.
verses.arminianNotes: Ephraim sends twenty thousand eight hundred, famous men in their fathers’ houses. Arminian readers note the large contribution from a powerful northern tribe, a sign of broad support for David.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the northern tribes joining David as part of God’s plan to unite Israel. Shared ground: the number is given as the text states it, and both traditions read it without speculating about its exactness.

verses.text: Of the half-tribe of Manasseh: eighteen thousand, who were mentioned by name, to come and make David king.
verses.arminianNotes: The half-tribe of Manasseh sends eighteen thousand, mentioned by name, to make David king. Arminian readers note that these men were designated for the task, perhaps chosen by their communities.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the phrase “mentioned by name” as stressing deliberate commitment to David. Both traditions read the verse as part of the list, while noting that the exact sense of being named is not explained.

verses.text: Of the children of Issachar, men who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do, their heads were two hundred; and all their brothers were at their command.
verses.arminianNotes: Issachar sends two hundred heads who understood the times and knew what Israel ought to do. Arminian readers see wisdom as a gift that leaders must use in making right decisions for the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see understanding of the times as discernment given by God for His people’s good. Shared ground: both traditions value the verse’s praise of wise leadership, while its exact meaning in context is discussed.

verses.text: Of Zebulun, such as were able to go out in the army, who could set the battle in array with all kinds of instruments of war: fifty thousand who could command and were not of double heart.
verses.arminianNotes: Zebulun sends fifty thousand skilled in battle and not of double heart. Arminian readers note the emphasis on undivided loyalty, a quality the Chronicler values highly in those who follow David.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see single-hearted devotion as a mark of those whom God brings to support His king. Both traditions read the phrase as praising wholehearted commitment, while the number is given as the text states it.

verses.text: Of Naphtali: one thousand captains, and with them with shield and spear thirty-seven thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Naphtali sends a thousand captains and thirty-seven thousand with shield and spear. Arminian readers note the substantial force from a distant northern tribe, showing the reach of David’s support.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers find it notable that Naphtali, near the northern border, supplies both officers and rank-and-file troops. The two figures are reported as written, with no attempt here to explain how they were reckoned.

verses.text: Of the Danites who could set the battle in array: twenty-eight thousand six hundred.
verses.arminianNotes: Dan sends twenty-eight thousand six hundred who could set the battle in array. Arminian readers note that the Danites are described in terms of their readiness for organized warfare.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the contribution of Dan as completing the picture of the northern tribes. Both traditions read the number as the text gives it, and note that large figures in Chronicles are interpreted in more than one way.

verses.text: Of Asher, such as were able to go out in the army, who could set the battle in array: forty thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Asher sends forty thousand able to go out in the army. Arminian readers note that Asher’s contribution, like the others, reflects a willingness to support David’s kingship with real resources.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the unanimous support of the tribes as a sign of God’s blessing on David. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the list, stating the number without further speculation.

verses.text: On the other side of the Jordan, of the Reubenites, the Gadites, and of the half-tribe of Manasseh, with all kinds of instruments of war for the battle: one hundred twenty thousand.
verses.arminianNotes: Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh from beyond the Jordan send one hundred twenty thousand. Arminian readers note the large contribution from the eastern tribes, often overlooked in other accounts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Chronicler’s concern to include the tribes east of the Jordan in all Israel. Both traditions state the number as given and note that the total of the list is very large, read differently by interpreters.

verses.text: All these were men of war who could order the battle array, and came with a perfect heart to Hebron to make David king over all Israel; and all the rest also of Israel were of one heart to make David king.
verses.arminianNotes: All these came with a perfect heart to Hebron, and the rest of Israel was of one heart to make David king. Arminian readers see willing, wholehearted participation by the people in recognizing God’s chosen king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the unity of Israel’s heart as the fruit of God’s purpose. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the climax of the list, emphasizing unity and wholehearted devotion as the Chronicler’s ideals.

verses.text: They were there with David three days, eating and drinking; for their brothers had supplied provisions for them.
verses.arminianNotes: They stay with David three days, eating and drinking, provided for by their brothers. Arminian readers note the celebration and generosity that mark the beginning of David’s reign over all Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the feast as a picture of covenant joy in God’s provision. Both traditions read the verse as showing that the coronation was a time of fellowship and shared abundance among the tribes.

verses.text: Moreover those who were near to them, as far as Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali, brought bread on donkeys, on camels, on mules, and on oxen: supplies of flour, cakes of figs, clusters of raisins, wine, oil, cattle, and sheep in abundance; for there was joy in Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Neighbors as far as Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali bring abundant food, for there was joy in Israel. Arminian readers note that the joy is shared widely, with people from distant tribes contributing generously.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see joy as the fitting response to God’s gift of a king after His own heart. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing verse as celebrating unity and blessing at the start of David’s reign over all Israel.
